text.p: India staged a mock plane hijacking on Thursday that left some senior officials confused until the government said it was only a drill to test security systems.
"It is a mock exercise. It was meant to test the systems," a government spokesman told Reuters.
Police and airline officials said Alliance Air flight 421A, carrying 29 passengers and six crew, was hijacked after it took off from New Delhi for the northern city of Jammu.
Alliance Air is a subsidiary of state-owned Indian Airlines.

Police in Jammu and Kashmir state initially said the Boeing 737, which left New Delhi at 3:15 p.m. (0945 GMT), had returned to the Indian capital after Pakistani authorities refused to allow it to land in the eastern city of Lahore.
Early reports about the mock hijacking confused even senior aviation officials.
At one point, Alliance Air managing director V. Kashyap told Reuters that he understood that the plane had been hijacked over the northern state of Punjab.
But authorities quickly denied the reports.

"There was a rumour that one Jammu-bound plane has been hijacked, but actually it was a mock exercise to get the response of the agencies involving anti-hijacking operations," a Civil Aviation Ministry spokeswoman told Reuters.
"The response was found to be good."

Keen to make the drill look realistic, authorities posted a sign at the Alliance Air counter saying: "Alliance Air flight 421A has been hijacked. For further information, kindly contact our control room."
Less than an hour after takeoff, the plane turned around over the northern state of Punjab and headed back to the capital, government officials said.

"The message for hijacking was given at 1605 hours (1035 GMT)," a Civil Aviation Ministry spokeswoman said. "The objective was to make it feel real, to check the effectiveness of the security systems."
At 4:30 p.m. (1100 GMT), the "hijackers" demanded to speak to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, the spokeswoman said. Thirty-five minutes later, the aircraft landed safely in Delhi.

Indian Airlines official Anoop Arora told Reuters that once on the ground, the mock hijackers released two passengers who had "fainted" and demanded that all vehicles be removed from around the aircraft, which was parked at a remote corner of the airport.
Asked if the mock hijackers were carrying guns, the Civil Aviation spokeswoman said: "Of course, it was an actual exercise."
Commandos rushed into the domestic airport terminal as police and paramilitary troops stood outside near a half-dozen fire trucks, witnesses said.
An hour and a half after the plane landed, security chiefs of Alliance Air and airport authorities were holding simulated negotiations with the "hijackers" in the airline terminal.
"I have been called but I do not know why," N.S. Verma, deputy chief of the anti-hijack commandos, told Reuters outside the airline terminal.
Air traffic controllers said they had known about the test of security systems before the aircraft took off but could not say who was on board.
